life_summary: Anthony Woodward Ivins was born September 16, 1852, in Toms River, New Jersey, to parents who had recently joined the LDS Church. His youth was marked by westward migration and pioneering life in the American frontier, settling in southern Utah. He developed practical skills in agriculture, land management, and indigenous relations that distinguished his career. Before his ecclesiastical prominence, Ivins served as mayor of St. George and as a prosecuting attorney and assessor, building a reputation as an able administrator and defender of Church interests. His intimate knowledge of southwestern frontier conditions and his diplomatic abilities made him a natural choice for leadership in developing the Church's Mexican communities and indigenous missionary work.
church_summary: Ivins served multiple missions to the American Southwest and Mexico (1875, 1877, 1882–1884), eventually becoming the first stake president in Mexico and overseer of Mexican Church affairs. He was ordained an apostle on October 6, 1907, and served in the Quorum of the Twelve until 1921, then as Second Counselor to Heber J. Grant (1921) and First Counselor (1925–1934). His mission work and presidency of the Southern States Mission established him as a bridge between the Anglo Mormon hierarchy and Spanish-speaking and Native American populations. He dedicated vast territories for missionary work and pioneered Church expansion into Mexico and the American South.
teaching_emphasis: Indigenous relations and Native American missionary efforts
